title: What Fortune Can Effect in Human Affairs and How to Withstand Her

questions.prompt: What share of action does Machiavelli give fortune in Chapter 25?
choices: About one-half
All of it
Only a tiny part

explanation.gentle: He says fortune is the arbiter of about one-half of our actions.
explanation.direct: The point is partial rule by fortune, not total fate or total control.
explanation.competitive: The chapter begins by splitting power instead of surrendering everything to chance.

questions.prompt: In the river metaphor, what should men do while the weather is fair?
choices: Wait to see how strong the next flood becomes
Build defenses and barriers
Trust the river to stay in its old channel

explanation.gentle: They should build defenses and barriers before the flood returns.
explanation.direct: Preparation in fair weather is the chapter's first answer to fortune.
explanation.competitive: The river metaphor makes agency matter before the violence begins.

questions.prompt: Why can a prince be happy today and ruined tomorrow without changing character?
choices: Because his advisers always become disloyal in time
Because fortune punishes every successful ruler eventually
Because the times changed while his fixed method did not

explanation.gentle: The chapter says ruin can come when the ruler's unchanged method no longer accords with the times.
explanation.direct: The problem is mismatch between style and moment, not necessarily moral decline.
explanation.competitive: A stable character can become politically disastrous once conditions stop rewarding it.

questions.prompt: A director sees a calm quarter ahead and debates whether to build backup capacity now or wait until volatility returns. Which response best fits Chapter 25?
choices: Use the calm to build the backup now
Wait until the first failure proves what is needed
Trust that stable conditions will continue if they have lasted this long

explanation.gentle: The chapter says barriers belong to fair weather, not to the middle of the flood.
explanation.direct: Preparation matters before fortune turns violent, not only after.
explanation.competitive: Waiting for proof often means giving fortune the easiest target.

questions.prompt: A student team keeps last semester's successful routine even after conditions become faster and more unstable. What is the best diagnosis from Chapter 25?
choices: The same method no longer fits the times
The team should never have valued routine at all
Their failure proves fortune rules everything

explanation.gentle: The chapter says methods succeed or fail by fit with the times.
explanation.direct: The issue is not that routine is always wrong, but that the old routine stopped matching the moment.
explanation.competitive: A method can remain disciplined and still become politically or practically misfitted.

questions.prompt: What does Julius II mainly prove in this chapter?
choices: That caution is always inferior to speed
That fortune cannot be resisted at all
That impetuosity succeeds when it fits the circumstances

explanation.gentle: Julius shows that boldness worked because the moment rewarded it.
explanation.direct: He is a case of fit, not a universal law that speed always wins.
explanation.competitive: The example is powerful precisely because Machiavelli says contrary times would have ruined the same man.

questions.prompt: Why is adaptation so difficult in Chapter 25?
choices: Because nature inclines men toward one method and prior success hardens that habit
Because rulers rarely know what their goals are
Because fortune punishes all change of course

explanation.gentle: Machiavelli says men rarely deviate from what nature inclines them to do, especially after succeeding that way.
explanation.direct: Past success makes course changes less likely, not more.
explanation.competitive: The real limit lies partly inside the ruler, not only outside him.

questions.prompt: What happens to the prince who relies entirely on fortune when fortune changes?
choices: He becomes more daring and therefore more secure
He is lost
He stays safe if his character remains constant

explanation.gentle: Machiavelli says directly that the prince who relies entirely on fortune is lost when it changes.
explanation.direct: The chapter attacks dependence on chance as a strategy.
explanation.competitive: Constancy of character is not enough when the ruler has built nothing and adapted nothing.

questions.prompt: How should Machiavelli's final preference for adventurousness be read?
choices: As proof that reckless speed is always the best policy
As a denial that barriers and preparation matter
As a judgment tied to times that may reward bold movement more than caution

explanation.gentle: The chapter's deeper rule is fit between method and times, so the closing preference is situational rather than universal.
explanation.direct: Machiavelli does prefer adventurousness, but after showing that circumstances determine which method works.
explanation.competitive: If you strip the preference away from the argument about changing times, you flatten the chapter into a slogan.

questions.prompt: If fortune governs only part of events, what best resists her in Chapter 25?
choices: Both barriers built beforehand and a willingness to change method when times shift
Barriers alone, because method never matters as much as structure
A single strong temperament applied consistently across all situations

explanation.gentle: The chapter needs both forms of resistance: advance preparation and adaptive fit.
explanation.direct: The river metaphor without the spirit-of-the-times rule is incomplete, and the adaptation rule without barriers is incomplete too.
explanation.competitive: Fortune is resisted partly by structure and partly by refusing to let one old method rule every new situation.
